title: Thunderstorm and Lightning Safety
description: Thunderstorms produce lightning, which can be deadly. Understanding lightning safety and knowing how to respond during thunderstorms can prevent injuries and fatalities.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Thunderstorms are weather systems characterized by the presence of lightning and its acoustic effect, thunder. Lightning is a sudden electrostatic discharge that occurs during a thunderstorm, producing a bright flash and loud sound. Lightning can strike up to 10 miles away from rainfall, and many lightning deaths occur ahead of storms or after storms have passed. India experiences frequent thunderstorms, especially during pre-monsoon and monsoon seasons. Lightning strikes are a significant cause of weather-related fatalities in the country.

sections.heading: Before a Thunderstorm
sections.content: Monitor weather forecasts and warnings. Secure outdoor objects that could be blown away or cause damage. Trim dead or rotting trees and branches that could fall on your home. Unplug sensitive electronic equipment to protect them from power surges. Have an emergency kit ready with flashlight, battery-powered radio, first aid supplies, and important documents. Identify safe shelter locations in your home. If you have a lightning protection system, ensure it is properly maintained. Know the difference between thunderstorm watches and warnings.

sections.heading: Indoor Safety During Thunderstorms
sections.content: Stay indoors and away from windows, doors, and porches. Do not use corded phones or electrical appliances—lightning can travel through electrical systems. Avoid contact with plumbing as lightning can travel through pipes. Do not wash hands, take showers, or do laundry during thunderstorms. Stay away from concrete floors and walls as they may contain metal reinforcement. Unplug expensive electronic equipment if possible. Do not lie on concrete floors or lean against concrete walls. Wait at least 30 minutes after the last thunder before resuming normal activities.

sections.heading: Outdoor Safety During Thunderstorms
sections.content: If you are outdoors and hear thunder, immediately move to a safe shelter. No place outside is safe during a thunderstorm. If you cannot reach a building, get inside a hard-topped metal vehicle and close the windows. Do not take shelter under isolated trees or in open fields. Avoid high ground, open spaces, and hilltops. Stay away from water, wet items, and metal objects such as fences, poles, and golf clubs. If you feel your hair stand on end or your skin tingle, crouch low on the balls of your feet, place your hands over your ears and head, and minimize contact with the ground.

sections.heading: Lightning Strike Response
sections.content: If someone is struck by lightning, call emergency services immediately. Lightning victims do not carry an electrical charge and are safe to touch. Check for breathing and pulse, and begin CPR if necessary. Treat burns by cooling them with water and covering with a clean dressing. Check for other injuries such as broken bones or hearing loss. Keep the victim calm and warm. Lightning can cause cardiac arrest, neurological damage, burns, and other injuries. Prompt medical attention is crucial for lightning strike victims.

sections.heading: Safety Precautions
sections.content: Follow the 30-30 rule: if the time between lightning flash and thunder is less than 30 seconds, seek shelter immediately. Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before leaving shelter. Do not resume outdoor activities until the storm has completely passed. Avoid open fields, beaches, and water bodies during thunderstorms. Stay away from metal objects and structures. Teach children about lightning safety. If you are caught in a group during a thunderstorm, spread out to reduce the risk of multiple casualties. Always prioritize safety over outdoor activities during thunderstorm warnings.
